theoryAdd.text: Going Deeper: Evaluating Expressions Step by Step

Precedence and associativity decide only how an expression is grouped, not the order in which its operands are computed. In a + b * c the multiplication is grouped first, but the compiler may fetch a, b and c in any order. Only four operators promise to finish their left operand first: &&, ||, ?: and the comma operator. Everywhere else, if a side effect (++, -- or an embedded assignment) changes a variable that another part of the same expression also reads or changes, as in i++ + i, the behaviour is undefined. A plain i = i + 1 is fine, because the store happens only after the right side has been computed.

theoryAdd.text: Mistakes that produce wrong answers in output questions:
items: ^ is exclusive OR, not a power: 2 ^ 3 is 1; two to the power 3 needs pow(2, 3) or 1 << 3.
a < b < c means (a < b) < c, which compares 0 or 1 with c (recent Clang versions even refuse to compile it); write a < b && b < c.
x & 4 != 0 and 1 << n + 1 group the wrong way; bracket every bitwise and shift sub-expression.
An assignment inside a condition, if (x = 0), stores 0 and is always false; if (x = 5) is always true.
(double)(a / b) casts too late: the integer division has already thrown the fraction away.
Shifting by a negative count or by at least the width of the type (1 << 32 for a 32-bit int) is undefined, and so is left-shifting a negative value.

theoryAdd.text: These have no defined output: i = i++;  a[i] = i++;  i++ + ++i;  printf("%d %d", i, i++);  INT_MAX + 1;  and integer division or % by zero. If one of them appears in an output question, the only correct choice is undefined behaviour (compiler dependent).

questions.explanation: Both operands are int, so 17 / 5 = 3.4 is truncated to 3. The remainder is 17 % 5 = 17 - 3 × 5 = 2.

C99 and C11 truncate the quotient toward zero (C89 left this implementation-defined), so -17 / 5 = -3.4 -> -3 (not -4). The remainder follows a % b = a - (a / b) × b: -17 - (-3 × 5) = -2 and 17 - (-3 × -5) = 2, so it takes the sign of the dividend.

questions.questionText: Which of the following expressions causes a compile error in C?
questions.explanation: The % operator requires integer operands; a floating-point remainder needs fmod() from <math.h>. The other three are legal and give 1, -1 and 3.5.
a / b * b groups left to right in int arithmetic: 9 / 4 = 2, then 2 × 4 = 8. The cast binds tighter than /, so (double)a / b = 9.0 / 4 = 2.25. r = 8 + 2.25 = 10.25.
* / % share one precedence level and group left to right: n % 10 = 9, n / 10 % 10 = 472 % 10 = 2 and n / 100 % 10 = 47 % 10 = 7. s = 9 + 2 + 7 = 18.
Relational, equality and logical operators produce an int: 1 for true and 0 for false. 5 > 3 is 1, 5 == 3 is 0 and !(5 < 3) is !0 = 1.
== groups left to right and yields 0 or 1: a == b == c is (a == b) == c = 1 == 5 = 0, while a == b == 1 is (5 == 5) == 1 = 1 == 1 = 1. C never reads a chain of comparisons the mathematical way.
i++ > 0 compares the old value 0, so it is false, and i becomes 1. Because the left side of || is false, the right side must be evaluated: j becomes 6 and 6 > 5 is true, so r = 1.

&& binds tighter than ||, so r = (a-- && b++) || ++c. a-- yields 1 (a becomes 0), so b++ is evaluated: it yields 0 (b becomes 1) and the && is false. The || therefore evaluates ++c, giving c = 6 (true), so r = 1.
&& has higher precedence, so the expression is x || (++y && ++y). x = 4 is true, so || stops at once: neither ++y runs, y stays 0, and z = 1 because logical operators produce 1, not the value 4.

questions.questionText: In C, what does a relational or logical expression such as a < b or a && b evaluate to?
options: A bool whose value is true or false
An int that may be any non-zero value when true
An int whose value is 1 (true) or 0 (false)
questions.explanation: C operators such as <, ==, && and ! give an int that is exactly 1 or 0. Any non-zero value counts as true when it is tested, but these operators always produce 1 for true.
12 = 1100 and 10 = 1010 in binary. AND keeps the common 1s: 1000 = 8; OR keeps every 1: 1110 = 14; XOR keeps the bits that differ: 0110 = 6.
x << n multiplies by 2^n: 3 × 2^4 = 48. x >> n divides a non-negative value by 2^n and drops the remainder: 100 / 8 = 12.5 -> 12.
In two's complement ~x = -x - 1, so ~12 = -12 - 1 = -13 and ~(-12) = 12 - 1 = 11. Flipping only the four bits of 1100 to get 0011 = 3 forgets that an int has 32 bits.
== has higher precedence than &, so the condition is x & (2 == 2) = 6 & 1 = 110 & 001 = 0, which is false. Writing (x & 2) == 2 would print yes.
Additive operators bind tighter than shifts, so the expression is 1 << (2 + 3) = 1 << 5 = 32, not (1 << 2) + 3 = 7.
0x5A = 0101 1010. f |= 1 sets bit 0: 0101 1011 (0x5B). f &= ~(1u << 4) clears bit 4: 0100 1011 (0x4B). f ^= 1u << 7 flips bit 7 from 0 to 1: 1100 1011 = 0xCB, printed by %X as CB.
Step by step: 10 + 5 = 15, 15 × 2 = 30, 30 - 4 = 26, and 26 / 3 = 8 because both operands are int.
A compound assignment evaluates its whole right side first: a *= 2 + 3 means a = a * (2 + 3) = 4 × 5 = 20, not a * 2 + 3 = 11.
x = 5 is an assignment, not a comparison: it stores 5 in x and the value of the expression, 5, is non-zero (true), so the if branch prints A 5.

questions.questionText: Given int x = 1, y = 2; which of the following statements causes a compile error?
questions.explanation: The left operand of an assignment must be a modifiable lvalue such as a variable. x + 1 is a computed value with no storage, so it cannot be assigned to. The others are a chained assignment, a chained compound assignment and a comma expression.
Assignment operators group right to left: a += (b *= (c -= 1)). First c = 4 - 1 = 3, then b = 3 × 3 = 9, then a = 2 + 9 = 11.
Post-decrement hands the old value 8 to the expression, so n = 8 - 3 = 5; afterwards m is 7.
++i increments first and yields 4; j-- yields the old value 3 and then j becomes 2. k = 4 × 3 = 12.
Each test uses the old i and then increments it. The tests 0, 1, 2 and 3 < 4 succeed and add the new values 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The failing test 4 < 4 still increments i, so i ends at 5.
The compiler always takes the longest possible token (maximal munch), so x+++y is read as (x++) + y: z = 5 + 2 = 7, x then becomes 6 and y is unchanged.

questions.questionText: When i++; and ++i; are each used as a complete statement on its own, how do they differ?
options: They have the same effect: each adds 1 to i
i++; leaves i unchanged and only ++i; increments it
++i; is not allowed as a stand-alone statement
They differ only when i is a float
questions.explanation: The difference between pre- and post-increment is only in the value the expression yields. When that value is not used, both simply add 1 to i.

options: The behaviour is undefined, because i is modified more than once without sequencing
questions.explanation: ++i, i++ and the assignment all modify i with no sequence point between them, so the behaviour is undefined and different compilers may print different values. Only output questions that modify each variable once per expression have a defined answer.
7 % 2 is 1, which is non-zero (true), so the conditional operator selects its second operand, the string "odd".
?: groups right to left, so the chain works like an else-if ladder: 65 >= 80 is false, 65 >= 60 is true, so g = 'B' and the remaining tests are never evaluated.
3 > 7 is false, so only the third operand b-- is evaluated: c receives the old value 7 and b becomes 6. The a++ in the unchosen branch never runs, so a stays 3.
?: has lower precedence than +, so y = x > 3 ? 10 : (20 + 1) = 10. In z the parentheses finish the conditional first, giving 10 + 1 = 11.
The comma operator evaluates left to right and yields its last operand: a += 3 makes a = 5, a * 2 is computed and thrown away, and a - 1 = 4 is stored in b.

Assignment binds more tightly than the comma operator, so x = a++, b + a; means (x = a++), (b + a): x gets 2, a becomes 3 and the value of b + a is thrown away. In y = (a++, b + a) the parentheses make the whole comma expression the value assigned; a becomes 4 before b + a is evaluated, so y = 5 + 4 = 9.
In c + 1 the char is promoted to int, so the size is 4. c = 'B' has the type of c (char, size 1), but sizeof never evaluates its operand, so the assignment never happens and c is still 'A'.

questions.questionText: Which statement about sizeof in C is correct?
options: It is a library function declared in <stdlib.h>
It is a preprocessor directive like #define
It returns the number of elements of any array passed to a function
It is a unary operator, normally worked out at compile time, that gives a size in bytes
questions.explanation: sizeof is a keyword operator that the compiler evaluates from the type of its operand (only variable-length arrays need run time), and its result has type size_t. Parentheses are required only around a type name, as in sizeof(int).

options: Compile error: signed and unsigned cannot be compared
questions.explanation: When an int meets an unsigned int, the int is converted to unsigned: -5 becomes 2^32 - 5 = 4,294,967,291, which is not less than 3, so the else branch runs.
Integer promotion converts both char operands to int before the addition, so 100 + 100 = 200 is computed in int and stored in the int s without any overflow.
Converting a floating value to int discards the fraction (truncation toward zero, not rounding down): (int)-3.7 = -3, (int)3.7 = 3 and (int)-0.5 = 0, so the second value is 3 + 0 = 3.
In u + i the int -3 is converted to unsigned, and the sum is taken modulo 2^32: 2 - 3 = -1 -> 4,294,967,295. That unsigned value is greater than 5, so the comparison gives 1.

questions.questionText: Given the declarations int i; float f; double d;, what is the type of the expression i * f + d?
questions.explanation: By the usual arithmetic conversions, i * f is computed as float, and float + double is computed as double, so the whole expression has type double.
* / % have equal precedence and group left to right: 3 * 4 = 12, 12 % 5 = 2 and 6 / 4 = 1 in integer division. Then 2 + 2 - 1 = 3.
From high to low the levels used are +, <<, &, |. So 1 + 2 = 3, 3 << 1 = 6, 6 & 7 = 6, and finally 8 | 6 = 1000 | 0110 = 1110 = 14. Reading strictly left to right would give 6.

questions.questionText: Which group of C operators associates from right to left?
options: Unary operators, the conditional operator ?: and the assignment operators
The logical operators && and || and the comma operator
questions.explanation: Unary operators (such as !, ~, prefix ++ and casts), ?: and every assignment operator group right to left, so a = b = c assigns c to b first. Almost all binary operators, including the comma, group left to right.

questions.questionText: Which of the following operators has the LOWEST precedence in C?
questions.explanation: The comma operator is at the very bottom of the precedence table, below the assignment operators, which are below ?:, which in turn is below ||.
